title: The First 10 Minutes
author: Jody Chan
summary: Jody Chan, writing after weeks spent observing early-career teachers establish their classroom routines, argues the first ten minutes of a lesson are disproportionately important for setting expectations, routines, and tone for everything that follows. She walks through her own scripted routine in granular detail: a fixed "do now" task on the board, positioning herself at the door to greet students individually, a stated silent period with a visible countdown, taking the register while circulating with a "magical marking pen" to check work, and repeating instructions consistently so every student is clear regardless of when they entered the room. Chan explains the reasoning behind each choice -- starting in silence calms students who arrive over-excited, retrieval-based "do now" questions draw on prior learning rather than just the previous lesson so absent students aren't penalised, and the visible clock keeps students aware of their own pacing. She frames the goal not as prescribing her exact routine for every teacher but as demonstrating the value of making every choice in those ten minutes deliberate and explicit rather than incidental. Chan closes with a five-point checklist for readers building their own version: plan the routine and environment deliberately, make the entry task achievable without explanation, consider introducing expectations incrementally, and script and rehearse the exact language used to give instructions.
points: Chan's \"do now\" retrieval questions deliberately draw on prior learning rather than just the previous lesson specifically so that students who were absent aren't penalised by content-specific starters.
Her routine embeds a visible clock and a stated time limit so students self-monitor their pacing during the silent starter period, rather than relying solely on teacher prompts.
Chan frames the goal as making every choice in the first ten minutes deliberate and explicit -- not prescribing her specific routine as the one correct version for all teachers.

Her five-point closing checklist -- plan deliberately, make the entry task achievable without explanation, consider incremental introduction, script and rehearse language -- gives the piece a reusable structure beyond her own classroom's specifics.
quotes: This first part of each lesson is crucial in setting your expectations, routines, grabbing students’ attention and setting the tone for the rest of the lesson.
I start practically every one of my lessons in the same way, so that students feel safe in knowing what to expect when they enter my room and so that it becomes habitual.
These are retrieval questions on prior learning, not just the last lesson in case students were absent.

I haven’t outlined my procedure above in the hopes that all teachers will copy everything I do in those first 10 minutes but rather to show how I have carefully thought about and made explicit everything that I want to happen in that time.
Script and practice saying want you want students to do, making your explanations clear and concise.
